So you're not allowed to steal each other's gold. That's stupid. Because now you don't really accomplish that much with warfare. For the longest time, this was the status quo. Then a man named Luga Zagazi came along. You can think of him as lower nobility. Within a city state, there is always conflict between upper and lower nobility. The upper nobility wants to maintain the status quo, while the lower nobility aims to steal power. This dynamic played out in Rome where Julius Caesar, from the lower nobility, stole power from the upper nobility.

Okay, these people are called ultimates. Lucas Leazi is one of them and he says, you know what, screw this; these rules are stupid. I want to conquer everyone and be the top dog. What he did was very different from previous times—he ransacked each city's temple. Now he had the capacity to build an empire. But by doing that, other city states saw him as a threat and invited mercenaries from Akad to help them. This led to the first world empire, the Aadian Empire, named by Sargon of Akid.

Now his name is interesting; it means legitimate ruler which probably tells us he's not a legitimate ruler but a mercenary like David who stole the throne. This pattern in history shows that when there's competition among city states, an outsider often unites them through innovations. The Qing dynasty united China because they were committed to total warfare—unlike the Jao or Chu or Wei. As you can see, the Aadian Empire stretched throughout the fertile crescent, conquering Mesopotamia (modern Iraq), extending to Anatolia and capturing much of the Levant.

The Levant is historically strategic; it gives access to Egypt, Mesopotamia, and Anatolia—three of the wealthiest regions. For most of history, this part was an Egyptian colony. But after the Bronze Age collapsed, Egypt couldn't project power in the Levant, leading different empires to fight for control. Jerusalem is literally the center of the world, considered so both religiously and geopolitically. This area is highly competitive because it's hard to protect Mesopotamia, which is very wealthy but threatened by mountain tribes.

Throughout history, whoever established an empire in Mesopotamia was always threatened by these borderlands. The Babylonian Empire gave us Hammurabi. Then came the Assyrian Empire, known for their brutality—they would kill everyone if you rebelled against them. Remember this pattern of empires changing due to threats from the borders.
